title: Young people’s experiences of nature in and outside school: implications for climate change and sustainability education
abstract: Young people’s perspectives on climate change, sustainability and nature reveal a set of interconnected yet uneven experiences that have significant implications for climate change and sustainability education. Drawing on a large-scale survey of 2,429 students aged 11–14 in England, this article examines how students’ nature connectedness shapes their attitudes towards learning about climate change and sustainability, and how their everyday encounters with nature – both within and outside school – inform these relationships. Students’ responses to open-ended questions illuminate the sensory, affective and relational qualities of nature that matter most to them, including aesthetic appreciation, emotional regulation and embodied experiences such as sound, smell and touch. Yet these rich accounts contrast sharply with their descriptions of nature in school, where experiences are often limited to incidental encounters during breaktimes or narrowly framed curricular activities. These disparities further highlight persistent social and spatial inequities in access to meaningful nature experiences, as well as missed opportunities within school environments to cultivate deeper forms of nature connection. The findings suggest that young people’s affective and sensory relationships with nature represent an underused lever for strengthening climate change and sustainability education. By foregrounding young people’s lived experiences, the article argues for a more integrated approach to learning in, about and for nature – one that recognises varied forms of nature engagement, attends to inequities in access, and positions enrichment as a holistic component of curriculum and personal development. The discussion considers how these insights can inform emerging policy agendas and support schools in designing climate and sustainability education that is both experientially grounded and responsive to young people’s diverse ways of knowing and relating to the natural world.

When subjective norms do not matter: an extended TPB model of social entrepreneurial intentions in Tunisia
abstract: Purpose This study aims to investigate the determinants of social entrepreneurial intentions (SEI) among Tunisian university students by integrating the theory of planned behavior (TPB) with individual psychological characteristics – risk-taking propensity, need for achievement and entrepreneurial self-efficacy. Moving beyond prior TPB applications, the authors situate our model within the distinct post-revolutionary Tunisian context and engage explicitly with the SEI literature, including constructs such as prosocial motivation and perceived social support. Design/methodology/approach A quantitative cross-sectional survey was conducted among 587 university students across five major Tunisian universities using stratified random sampling. Data were analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling. Measurement scales were validated through a systematic cultural adaptation process, including translation, back-translation, expert review and a pilot test with 42 participants. Findings SEI are primarily driven by entrepreneurial self-efficacy (ß = 0.34, p < 0.001, f² = 0.31), attitude toward social entrepreneurship (ß = 0.21, p < 0.001, f² = 0.15) and perceived behavioral control (ß = 0.18, p < 0.001, f² = 0.12). Risk-taking propensity and need for achievement exert small but significant direct effects. Subjective norms show no significant influence, a finding theoretically explained through post-revolutionary individualization processes in Tunisia. The model explains 64.2% of the variance in SEI. Practical implications Universities should design experiential SEI programs to build self-efficacy. Policymakers should reduce institutional barriers by integrating social entrepreneurship into Tunisia’s National Employment Strategy 2030, supporting student incubators through NGO partnerships and creating seed-funding mechanisms specific to social ventures. Originality/value This study contributes to the underexplored SEI literature in Tunisia by demonstrating how post-revolutionary individualization reshapes classic TPB relationships, particularly the non-effect of subjective norms in a nominally collectivistic culture. Theoretically, this refines TPB by specifying a boundary condition under which subjective norms lose predictive power. It also extends the SEI construct operationalization to include moral obligation and perceived social support dimensions, advancing measurement rigor in this setting.

Understanding the factors influencing social entrepreneurial intentions among Indian youth: a multi-group analysis
journal: Journal of Enterprising Communities: People and Places in the Global Economy
abstract: Purpose This study aims to forecast university students’ intentions towards social entrepreneurship (SE). The research investigated the individual entrepreneurial orientation (IN-EO) dimensions and contextual factors that shape the intentions of Generation Z (business and engineering students) using gender like a control variable. Design/methodology/approach The data was gathered from 438 engineering and 412 business students in north-west India using a questionnaire which was self-administered. The data was further analysed using multi-group analysis following measurement invariance of composite model steps, PROCESS function and partial least square-structural equation modelling. Findings The outcomes showcased that IN-EO factors positively shaped engineering and business students’ social entrepreneurial intentions (SEI). The result of the study confirms that university support strongly influences engineering students but insignificantly influences business students towards SE. In contrast, both groups represented an insignificant association between perceived social support (PSS) in the context of SEI. Originality/value The study addressed a knowledge gap by investigating how IN-EO dimensions, university support and PSS influences SEI. The study also showcases on the significance of nation for establishing an increased supportive atmosphere to encourage scholars to explore SE as a feasible career choice.

title: The myth of the algorithmic entrepreneur: how gig platforms quietly close the door on worker learning
journal: Development and Learning in Organizations: An International Journal
abstract: Purpose This viewpoint examines how two mechanisms of entrepreneurial identity and opacity in algorithmic management (AM) systems operate jointly to suppress learning and developmental capacity in app-based gig platforms. Design/methodology/approach This viewpoint is based on a review of existing research on gig work, AM, and workplace learning. It draws insights from prior studies and presents them in a practitioner-oriented format. Findings Entrepreneurial framing puts the burden of problem diagnosis on individual workers, which makes learning more difficult. At the same time, algorithmic opacity undermines the conditions under which informal learning can occur. Together, these mechanisms create a system in which workers are not positioned to claim learning and development as a right. Research limitations/implications This viewpoint extends gig work research by bringing workplace learning into the discussion. Future studies can examine how entrepreneurial identity and algorithmic management together shape workers’ learning and developmental outcomes, rather than studying them separately. It also encourages HR and organizational scholars to examine learning as an organizational responsibility in platform work. Practical implications Three interventions are proposed: retiring the entrepreneurial label, redesigning feedback systems, and building developmental infrastructure independent of platform control. Originality/value This viewpoint offers a framework to understand how and what ideological and structural mechanisms hinder workers’ developmental capacity. It goes beyond existing critiques by showing how these mechanisms interact, rather than treating them as separate problems.

title: Examining the effect of tax avoidance on ESG performance: moderating role of audit fees
journal: Journal of Economic and Administrative Sciences
abstract: Purpose This study explores the effect of corporate tax avoidance (TA) on environmental, social, and governance performance (ESG_P), emphasizing the moderating role of audit fees (AF). While TA can provide financial flexibility to support sustainability initiatives, it also raises concerns about ethical conduct and transparency. The study seeks to clarify whether TA promotes or undermines ESG outcomes and how audit quality, as reflected in AF, influences this relationship. Design/methodology/approach The analysis is based on 602 firm-year observations from FTSE 100 non-financial companies over the period 2014–2022. Using a panel data regression framework, the study examines both the direct impact of TA on ESG_P and the moderating effect of AF. To address potential endogeneity and enhance the robustness of the findings, a dynamic panel estimation approach (system GMM) is employed, supported by comprehensive diagnostic and robustness tests. Findings The results reveal a significant positive association between TA and ESG_P, suggesting that firms may reinvest tax savings into sustainability-related initiatives. However, this relationship weakens under higher AF, indicating that stronger audit scrutiny limits opportunistic tax behavior and enhances corporate transparency. Originality/value This study contributes to the growing literature on corporate sustainability by revealing the dual nature of TA, both as a potential driver of ESG investment and as a governance risk. By incorporating AF as a moderating factor, the research provides novel evidence on how external audit quality can align tax strategies with authentic sustainability objectives.
